svg.title: The discovery chain: two entry points, one metadata document
svg.desc: Four panels. Panel A, the fast path: an unauthenticated POST to the MCP endpoint is answered 401, and the client fetches the URL named in the WWW-Authenticate header, whose resource_metadata parameter is printed underneath in full. Panel B, drawn the same size because a client is required to be able to follow either route, is the fallback when no such header arrives: probe the well-known protected-resource path with the resource path inserted first, then the same well-known path at the root, where a 404 is normal for a server that lives on a path. Panel C prints the protected resource metadata document and runs one arrow out of each of its four fields to the single job that field has: resource is the audience the token must name, authorization_servers names who may issue tokens you accept and needs at least one entry, scopes_supported is a published minimum rather than a whole catalog, and bearer_methods_supported says the token travels in a header and never a query string. A note adds that the client sends that resource value back in both the authorization request and the token request, which is how the token ends up naming you. Panel D shows the client repeating the same trick one hop further out against the authorization server's own metadata, trying the OAuth 2.0 well-known path first and OpenID Connect discovery second.
svg.text: A server must publish one of the entry points. A client must be able to follow both.
A. The 401 tells you where to look
No guessing, one round trip. The SDK writes this header for you.
B. No header, so probe these, in order
well-known inserted between the host and your path
the root; a 404 here is normal for a server on a path
C. One document, and the one job each field has
the audience your token must name
who may issue tokens you accept; at least one
your published minimum, not your whole catalog
a header, never a query string
The client sends resource=<that value> in both the authorization request and the token request. That is how the token names you.
D. Then the same trick at the authorization server, in this order
